title_vi: Tường lửa: sáu cách viết một luật

source_snapshot.note: Pinned commit/path body independently hashed as Git blob; computed OID matches provider tree OID. Non-empty source was read; no source-image bytes used.

related.reason_vi: Tường lửa theo dõi trạng thái và các loại tường lửa.

claims.evidence: Source read; behaviour of each rule type observed by running nftables v1.0.9 on loopback ports 18091-18099 (table deleted afterwards, no leftover table); no nftables documentation page was reachable, so rule semantics rest on those runs; ICMP, time zones, real window changes, address spoofing and content-based application identification were not tested.

mobile.evidence: Chromium (Playwright) rendered the full lesson at each width with optional sections open; diagram scale measured from the rendered image and every SVG text box checked against the viewBox. Not learner testing and not GitHub or a real phone.

claims.claim_vi: The source lists six firewall use cases: port-based rules (for example allow only 80 and 443 for web browsing), IP address filtering (allow or deny by source or destination address, with trusted addresses whitelisted and known malicious ones blacklisted), protocol-based rules (TCP, UDP, ICMP; for example only TCP on port 22), time-based rules (different access during business hours and after hours), stateful inspection (monitor active connections and allow traffic only if it matches an established connection) and application-based rules (allow or block specific applications such as Skype or BitTorrent).

Observed: with a rule accepting TCP destination port 18091 and a rule dropping ports 18092 and 18093, a connection to 18091 returned its banner and a connection to 18092 timed out; after the rules were replaced by one accepting 18093, a service that is not HTTP and listens on 18093 answered. A port rule matches the number, not the application behind it.
claims.verified_by: Linux nftables v1.0.9 on loopback with a throw-away table that was deleted afterwards; No external page reports this output; observed by executing the code on the authoring machine.

claims.claim_vi: Observed: a rule dropping TCP to port 18091 from source 127.0.0.2 blocked a client bound to 127.0.0.2 (timeout) and let a client from 127.0.0.1 through; an allow-list (accept source 127.0.0.1, then drop the rest) gave the same two results.
claims.verified_by: Linux nftables v1.0.9 on loopback with a throw-away table that was deleted afterwards; No external page reports this output; observed by executing the code on the authoring machine.

claims.claim_vi: Observed: a rule 'meta l4proto udp ip daddr 127.0.0.1 drop' with no port blocked UDP exchanges to two different ports (18094 and 18098, both timed out) while a TCP connection to port 18095 on the same address still worked. ICMP was not tested (ping was not installed).
claims.verified_by: Linux nftables v1.0.9 on loopback with a throw-away table that was deleted afterwards; No external page reports this output; observed by executing the code on the authoring machine.

claims.claim_vi: Observed: a rule 'tcp dport 18096 meta hour "HH:MM"-"HH:MM" drop' blocked the connection when the window (30 minutes either side) contained the machine's clock (UTC, 14:22) and let it through when the window was two hours later. How time zones are handled was not tested.
claims.verified_by: Linux nftables v1.0.9 on loopback with a throw-away table that was deleted afterwards; No external page reports this output; observed by executing the code on the authoring machine.

claims.claim_vi: Observed (a window opening is simulated by adding the drop rule while a connection is open): with only a drop rule, a connection sending a line every 0.25 s delivered 7 lines in the 1.5 s before the rule and 1 line in the 2.0 s after; with 'ct state established,related accept' placed before the drop, it delivered 7 and then 8 lines. A new connection to the port was blocked in both cases. Rule order decides whether an open connection survives.
claims.verified_by: Linux nftables v1.0.9 on loopback with a throw-away table that was deleted afterwards; No external page reports this output; observed by executing the code on the authoring machine.

claims.claim_vi: Observed in the output hook: a rule 'tcp dport 18097 meta skuid 65534 drop' blocked a client started as uid 65534 (timeout) and let the same program run as root through. This distinguishes the local user that sends the packet, not the program name or the content, so it is a host-firewall approximation of application control and not the content-based identification of applications such as Skype that the source describes.
claims.verified_by: Linux nftables v1.0.9 on loopback with a throw-away table that was deleted afterwards; No external page reports this output; observed by executing the code on the authoring machine.

claims.claim_vi: Address spoofing, stale blacklists and shared addresses weakening IP rules, the cost of looking deeper than ports, and the way next-generation firewalls recognise applications are the author's general knowledge and were not tested or checked against a standard.

design_notes_vi: Một thẻ nêu luật là điều kiện cộng hành động, sáu thẻ kiểu luật mỗi thẻ ghi thứ luật nhìn vào và một giới hạn, một thẻ đỏ nêu thứ tự luật. Không dùng ảnh nguồn.
source_deviations: The source's protocol-rule example (only TCP on port 22) combines a protocol and a port; the lesson shows a protocol rule with no port.
The source presents time-based rules as a schedule; the lesson adds that an already open connection survives or not depending on rule order.

The source's application-based rules name applications such as Skype and BitTorrent; the lesson could only test a user-based rule on one host and says that content-based identification was not tested.
The source's stateful inspection entry is shortened to a pointer to the earlier lesson sd-14-007, which already holds the nftables run.
editorial_note_vi: Bài mới viết trong kho này, chờ review kỹ thuật. Chưa user testing hoặc phê duyệt phát hành.
